paragraphs: A king used to put the same question to every monk who passed through his land: who is greater, the one who gives up the world, or the one who lives in it and does his duty? Whoever said the monk was greater and could not prove it was ordered to marry. Whoever said the householder was greater and could not prove it was ordered the same. Finally a young sannyasin answered that each is equally great in his own place. Asked for proof, he told the king to come and live as he did for a few days.

They travelled until they reached a great kingdom where drums were beating and a crier announced that the princess would choose a husband. By custom, princes and nobles paraded before her as she was carried past on a throne; she would garland the one she chose. This princess, the most beautiful in the world, wanted the handsomest man, and none had pleased her yet. This gathering was the grandest of all, and once again it seemed headed for failure.

Then she saw a young sannyasin, radiant as the sun, quietly watching from a corner. She stopped and threw her garland over him. He tossed it off: he was a monk, what did he want with marriage? Her father, thinking him too poor to dare, offered half the kingdom now and all of it later. The monk threw off the garland again and walked away. The princess, now hopelessly in love, followed him, and the king and his guide followed her at a distance.

Deep in a forest the young monk slipped away along paths he knew well. The princess sat under a tree and wept. The king and the sannyasin comforted her: it was too dark now, but in the morning they would show her the way out. They rested under a large tree.

In that tree lived a little bird with his wife and three chicks. He worried that guests had come on a winter night and there was no fire. So he fetched a burning twig, and the travellers built a blaze. Then he worried that they had nothing to eat; as householders, feeding guests was their duty. He dived into the fire and died. His wife, unwilling to let his effort be wasted, followed him. Then the three chicks, seeing it still was not enough, jumped in too. The stunned travellers could not eat them and went hungry. At dawn they led the princess home.

Then the sannyasin turned to the king. Live in the world like those birds, always ready to give yourself for others. Renounce it like that young monk, to whom beauty and a kingdom were nothing. Each is great in his own place, but one's duty is not the other's.
learn: There isn't one 'best' path in life: a career, a family or a life of service can each be noble. What matters is living your chosen path fully and honestly, and not judging someone whose role is different from yours.
